body:
This passage frames the whole chapter. Everything taught so far serves some people directly for liberation — they hear the compendium and are free. Others can only use it once initiation is on the table. So initiation, and what follows from it, must now be taught. And the first question is eligibility: who is entitled to receive it? That question is not procedural (who may be initiated) but causal (what makes one capable of receiving it) — and it forces the topic of this ahnika: the descent of power. Nothing is yet asserted about grace; the question is opened, not answered, and the pūrvapakṣa follows.

The passage has two sentences and one question. First, the frame: what was taught so far reaches some directly for liberation in the stated compendium manner; for others, it reaches only through coming into use in the initiation to be taught. Hence initiation and the rest must be taught. The "and the rest" (dīkṣādikam) signals that initiation is the door to a whole sequence (snāna, yāga, putraka, sadyaḥ, parokṣa, liṅgoddhāra, abhiṣeka, antyeṣṭi, conduct) that follows in A12–A20. Second, the question: "who is the entitled one?" (kaḥ adhikārī) — and for that determination (nirūpaṇārtham), the descent of power is examined (śaktipāto vicāryate). The shift from "who may be initiated" to "what makes one capable" is the ahnika's pivot: eligibility is not a permission but a causal capacity, and the cause of that capacity is śaktipāta. Nothing is yet asserted about grace; the question is opened and the pūrvapakṣa (three theories) follows in P2.
terms: adhikārin (entitled recipient), apavarga (liberation), saṃgraha-nīti (compendium manner), vaktavyam (must be taught), vicāryate (is examined).
see_also: A10 (kalādhvā), A12 (snāna, bath before initiation), spans TS11.1–11.2.
function: Frame-setting and topic-introduction. Establishes why śaktipāta, not initiation itself, is the ahnika's subject, and why eligibility is a causal question.
local_context: Opening of the ahnika; follows A10's kalādhvā (digit-course) and precedes the pūrvapakṣa in P2.
boundary: No doctrine stated; the pūrvapakṣa theories follow in P2. No unresolved items beyond the frame.

body:
Three theories of descent are proposed and each demolished. First, the knowledge-theory: saṃsāra is ignorance-rooted, so when knowledge dawns, power descends. But "the dawn of right knowledge" is itself the unexplained term (the charge is promissory here — iti vācyam); and if karma-produced, enjoyment-contingency (bhogatva-prasaṅga) and over-extension (atiprasaṅga) follow; if Lord's-will-caused, mutual dependence (anyonyāśrayatā), futility (vaiyarthya), and passion in the Lord (rāgādi-prasaṅga). Second, the karma-equilibrium theory: equal opposed karmas deadlock, grace slips through. But succession excludes opposition; a third unopposed karma would still deliver pleasure; or the body should fall on the spot. The "whence?" (kutaḥ?) marks the point: no theory can state its own ground. Third, stain-maturation (P3). Each proposal collapses under its own consequences.

Abhinava does not argue against grace but against every proposed mechanism of grace. The knowledge-theory is circular: samyak-jñānodaya is itself "defective" (vikṛta) — the charge is promissory here (iti vācyam), answered later. If grace is karma-produced, it inherits action's limits: like any reward, it would be merely enjoyed, and anyone enjoying anything would count as graced — the concept explodes (atiprasaṅga). If grace comes from the Lord's will, knowledge's dawn either grounds the will (circular again) or floats free of it (pointless) — while saddling the Lord with motive and partiality (rāgādi-prasaṅga). The karma-equilibrium theory: when two equal and opposed deeds deadlock, their equilibrium lets grace through. But deadlock needs simultaneity; deeds ripen in sequence, where "opposition" has no grip (kramikatve virodhāyogāt). And even granted the deadlock, some third, unopposed deed would still be delivering its pleasures (bhogadāna-prasaṅga) — or, if no deed is operating at all, the body should drop on the spot (dehapāta-prasaṅga). Plead that birth-and-lifespan deeds run on while only pleasure-deeds jam: on what ground? (kutaḥ?) If the deed-structure is intact, what exactly would descending power be afraid of in the pleasure-giver? The repeated "whence?" marks the point: no theory can state its own ground.
terms: karmasāmya (equilibrium of karma), atiprasaṅga (over-extension), anyonyāśraya (mutual dependence), vaiyarthya (futility), kramikatva (succession), jātyāyuṣprada (birth-and-lifespan-giving).
function: Pūrvapakṣa demolition. Clears the ground for the siddhānta in P4 by showing that no proposed mechanism (knowledge, karma, equilibrium) can account for grace.
local_context: Immediately after the framing (P1); the siddhānta begins at P4.
boundary: The "defective" charge against right knowledge is promissory (iti vācyam); answered in later ahnikas. kiṃsvarūpa/kiṃnimitta hang until P3/P4.

body:
"Grace comes when the stain ripens." The challenge stands: what is this ripening — what is it, and what causes it? The whole catalogue of proposed causes (dispassion, merit, discernment, good company, attainment, worship) is refuted. For dualist schools, every option on the table is incoherent. The theory cannot state its own nature, cause, or means — the same move as P2 but aimed at a single theory. The hetu-list refutation shows that no moral or ritual achievement causes grace; hence grace is not merit-earned.

"At-the-maturation-of-stain, the descent" — but that too: of what nature is it, and what is its cause? (kiṃsvarūpaḥ? kiṃ ca tasya nimittam?) No answer comes. And with it fall the whole catalogue of supposed causes — dispassion (vairāgya), special dharma (dharmaviśeṣa), discrimination (viveka), service of the good (satsevā), attainment of the good (satprāpti), worship of gods (devapūjā) and the rest — refuted (pratyukta). Thus, for dualists (bhedavādin), everything is incoherent (sarvam asamañjasam). The theory cannot state its own nature, cause, or means — the same move as P2 but aimed at a single theory. The hetu-list refutation shows that no moral or ritual achievement causes grace; hence grace is not merit-earned. This is the pūrvapakṣa's last stand; the siddhānta opens at P4 with autonomy.
terms: malaparipāka (stain-maturation), kiṃsvarūpa (of what nature), kiṃnimitta (what cause), hetu (cause), bhedavāda (dualism), asamañjasa (incoherent).
function: Closes the pūrvapakṣa. The siddhānta begins at P4.
local_context: P2–P3 are the refutation half; P4 opens the siddhānta.
boundary: Nature and cause questions left hanging — answered only by the coming siddhānta (P4). The "defective" charge (P2) also remains promissory.

body:
Abhinava's own position, and it needs no patch from the wreckage above. The Lord, playing at hiding himself, has become the bound soul, the person, the atom — and place, time, and particular nature don't contradict this, since they are his own display. In exactly the same way, when the hiding lifts and one's own nature is recovered — in a flash or by degrees — the atom becomes what we call "a recipient of the descent." And the one from whom it descends is supreme Śiva, whose whole essence is autonomy. So the descent, whose fruit is simply nature showing itself, is unconditioned. Qualifications follow the fruit, not the mechanism: wanting pleasure? Then karma conditions apply. Wanting a higher pleasure? Then the very same descent comes down through Rudra, Viṣṇu, Brahmā — the lords posted inside Māyā's womb at the Lord's will — wearing the shape of mantra and the rest, teaching apart Māyā from person, person from power, from nature, from intellect, and barring the way down to a lower enjoyment. Wanting both pleasure and freedom? Then conditioned in the pleasure, unconditioned in the freedom — both at once. "But why this person and not that?" The question assumes a "person" standing outside being, waiting to be picked. There is none: the Lord shines this way, and that shining is all there is. The descent is ninefold — intense, moderate, mild, each in excess, middle, and deficient measure. At the peak of intensity, the body drops and there is identity with the Lord then and there. At middle intensity, intuitive knowledge dawns needing no book and no teacher, self-certifying — and with it the intuitive teacher, who gives pleasure and freedom with no outer rite at all. Such a one is bound by no observance. Yet ranks remain, because will differs: even the intuitive may honor scripture, for agreement's sake — which is why the books describe the intuitive teacher in many forms, grounded and groundless. In every case the intuitive share outweighs; where it is present, nothing else confers standing.

The passage moves in six steps. (1) The play-analogy: the Lord, playing at hiding himself, has become the bound soul, the person, the atom — and place, time, and particular nature don't contradict this, since they are his own display. (2) In exactly the same way, when the hiding lifts and one's own nature is recovered — in a flash or by degrees — the atom becomes what we call "a recipient of the descent." (3) The one from whom it descends is supreme Śiva, whose whole essence is autonomy; so the descent, whose fruit is simply nature showing itself, is unconditioned. (4) Qualifications follow the fruit, not the mechanism: pleasure → karma-conditioned; higher pleasure → conditioned through Rudra/Viṣṇu/Brahmā (Māyā-womb lords, Lord's-will-impelled, teaching apart Māyā/person/power/nature/intellect, barring lower enjoyment); both → conditioned in pleasure, unconditioned in freedom. (5) "But why this person and not that?" — the question assumes a "person" standing outside being, waiting to be picked; there is none: the Lord shines this way, and that shining is all there is. (6) The ninefold typology (11.7): intense/moderate/mild × excess/middle/deficiency — with distinct fates (utmost-intense → dehapāta = parameśatā; middle-intense → prātibhajñāna, sacrament-free prātibha-guru; gradation persists via icchāvaicitrya; pratibhāṃśa decisive over others).
terms: svātantrya (autonomy), śaktipāta-pātra (recipient of descent), prātibha (intuitive), nirapekṣa (unconditioned), sāpekṣa (conditioned), navadhā (ninefold), icchāvaicitrya (will-diversity), saṃnidhi (presence).
function: Core doctrine of the ahnika. Establishes the autonomy-grounded, fruit-graded typology of descent (ninefold) and dissolves the selection problem.
local_context: P1–P3 refuted; P4–P10 build the siddhānta.
boundary: nirbhitti/sabhitti teacher-forms per scriptures (external). "Nature" renders svarūpa + prakṛti (AQ-3, L1 revision note). The "defective" charge (P2) remains promissory.

body:
The same pattern holds among the liberated ones: a mild-intense descent moves them to want a true teacher; toward a false teacher there is only further concealment; and the move from false to true is itself descent's effect. The true teacher knows this scripture's principles whole — he is Lord Bhairava in person. A yogin too can liberate by well-practised knowledge; worldly fitness (luck, charm, credentials) is as irrelevant as good looks are to arithmetic. A false teacher is anyone else.

The passage moves in three steps. (1) The same pattern among liberated ones: where Śiva's presence is beginningless, a mild-intense descent moves them to create and dissolve — and to want a true teacher. Toward a false teacher there is only further hiding (tirobhāva eva); and even the move from a false teacher to a true one is itself from the descent (śaktipātād eva). (2) The true teacher: full of the knowledge of the principles of all this scripture (samastaitacchāstratattvajñānapūrṇaḥ) — Lord Bhairava the Blessed himself (sākṣāt bhagavadbhairavabhaṭṭārakaḥ eva). Even a yogin, by well-practised knowledge alone (svabhyastajñānatayaiva), has liberating power (mocakatve); therein, fitness (yogyatva) is useless, like possession of good fortune, charm, and the rest (saubhāgyalāvaṇyādimattvasya iva) — the arithmetic analogy unpacked in L2. (3) The false teacher is simply everyone else (anyaḥ sarvaḥ eva).
terms: sadguru (true teacher), asadguru (false teacher), saubhāgya (good fortune/charm), mocakatva (liberating power), yogyatva (fitness).
function: Teacher-criterion. Separates authority (fullness of knowledge) from office or worldly qualification.
local_context: Follows P4's ninefold typology; P6 takes up initiation.
boundary: None major. The saubhāgya-irrelevance is stated by analogy; its force is rhetorical, not argued.

body:
So the seeker receives from the teacher the initiation whose mark is knowledge — and is free at once, while still alive. It comes by a glance, a word, a text taught, a conduct shown, food shared, and more. There is also the initiation that severs the life-breath — but that one is for the hour of death, as will be taught. From the highest three intensities of the intense, even the initiated has no steady footing in his own Śiva-nature — but as conviction ripens, at the body's end he is Śiva, no qualification. From the middle of the moderate: still hungry for pleasure, yet a fit vessel for knowledge in that very initiation — he enjoys, with this same body, through yoga practice, and at the body's end he is Śiva.

The passage moves in four steps. (1) The wisher obtains from the teacher the knowledge-characterized initiation (jñānalakṣaṇāṃ dīkṣām), by which he is liberated instantly (sadyaḥ eva), even while alive (jīvann api). The varieties: by glance (avalokanāt), by speech (kathanāt), by scriptural instruction (śāstrasambodhanāt), by showing of conduct (caryādarśanāt), by giving of food (carudānāt), and more (ityādayo bhedāḥ). (2) Or the practitioner then instantly obtains the life-severing initiation (prāṇaviyojikāṃ dīkṣām) — but that is to be performed only at the moment of death (maraṇakṣaṇa eva kāryā), as will be taught (iti vakṣyāmaḥ) — deferred to A15/A19. (3) From the utmost three intensities of the intense descent of power (tīvrās tridhā utkṛṣṭamadhyāt): even one who is initiated (kṛtadīkṣāko 'pi) has no firm conviction of the Śiva-nature of his own self (svātmanaḥ śivatāyām na tathā dṛḍhapratipattiḥ); but by the maturation of conviction (pratipattiparipākakrameṇa), at the end of the body (dehānte) he is Śiva indeed (śivaḥ eva). (4) From the middle moderate (madhyamadhyāt): though desiring Śiva-hood (śivatotsuko 'pi), he desires enjoyment (bhogaprepsuḥ) — he is a fit vessel of knowledge (jñānabhājanam) in that same initiation (tathaiva dīkṣāyām); and he, by the practice of yoga (yogābhyāsa), having enjoyed enjoyment (bhuktvā bhogam) with this very body (anenaiva dehena), at the body's end (dehānte) is Śiva indeed (śivaḥ eva).
terms: jñānalakṣaṇā dīkṣā (knowledge-characterized initiation), prāṇaviyojikā (life-severing initiation), maraṇakṣaṇa (moment of death), dṛḍhapratipatti (firm conviction), pratipattiparipāka (maturation of conviction), jñānabhājana (fit vessel of knowledge).
see_also: A11 P4, A12 (snāna), A15 (sadyaḥ), spans TS11.11–11.13.
function: Initiation-types and grade→fate mapping. Establishes that grade determines timing and mode, never the outcome for the entitled.
local_context: P4–P5 established descent and teacher; P6 takes up the rite.
boundary: Prāṇaviyojikā rite deferred (iti vakṣyāmaḥ → A15/A19). The "fit vessel" (jñānabhājana) criterion is asserted, not argued.

body:
One step down from the middle moderate: pleasure enjoyed in another body, then Śiva-hood. The moderate is threefold; where hunger for pleasure rules, the grade is mild — for that hunger travels by the Lord's mantra and yoga, which end in freedom, so the structure still counts as descent. Three sub-ranks within, by the same gradation. This whole mild-to-intense span terminating in freedom is the principal descent (mukhya śaktipāta).

The passage moves in three steps. (1) From deficient-moderate (nikṛṣṭamadhyāt): having enjoyed enjoyment (bhuktvā bhogam) with another body (dehāntareṇa), he attains Śiva-hood (śivatvam eti). (2) The moderate is threefold (madhyas tu tridhā): when eagerness for enjoyment is predominant (bhogotsukatā pradhānabhūtā), then there is mildness (mandatvam) — since eagerness there is by way of the Lord's mantra and yoga as means (pārameśvaramantrayogopāyatayā yatas tatra autsukyam), and since from mantra and yoga of the Lord there is ending in liberation (pārameśamantrayogādeś ca yato mokṣaparyantatvam), hence there is descent-nature (ataḥ śaktipātarūpatā). (3) There too, through gradation (tāratamyāt), there is threefoldness (traividhyam). Thus this — the whole mild-to-intense span terminating in freedom — is the principal descent (ity eṣaḥ mukhyaḥ śaktipātaḥ). "Principal" unpacks in L2: the full operative span, not a single grade.
terms: nikṛṣṭamadhya (deficient-moderate), madhyas tridhā (moderate threefold), bhogotsukatā (eagerness for enjoyment), mandatva (mildness), mukhya śaktipāta (principal descent), tāratamya (gradation).
function: Completes the grade table (utmost/middle/deficient × intense/moderate/mild); defines mukhya śaktipāta.
local_context: P6 gave utmost/middle; P7 closes the moderate band and defines "principal."
boundary: None major. The "principal" gloss is a register choice, flagged for review.

body:
What of the Vaiṣṇavas and the rest? Their grace is like the king's favor — real, but no ending in freedom; so no analysis here. Lord-and-Śakti present everywhere, but not as "the eldest" — she is Fierce, and Fiercer. The descent varies: samayin/five-streams Vaiṣṇava → highest charge of the sixfold word; leap-course; no stages. Lower-lower teachers have no standing; an upper teacher, by completeness, enlivens even the lowest. Five teacher-names for one plenitude; without him no initiation succeeds.

The passage moves in four steps. (1) Outsiders: for Vaiṣṇavas and the rest, as with royal favor (rājānugrahavat), there is no ending in liberation (na mokṣāntatā) — hence no analysis here (na iha vivecanam). (2) Lord-and-Śakti presence everywhere (śivaśaktyadhiṣṭhānam sarvatra), as stated; but that is not the eldest (na jyeṣṭhā), rather fierce or fiercer (ghorā ghoratarā vā). (3) The descent varies (vicitro 'pi), divides by variety of gradation (tāratamyavaicitryāt): some Vaiṣṇava-dweller (kaścid vaiṣṇavādisthaḥ), by samayin-course (samayyādikrameṇa), in the five-streams (srotaḥpañcake), attaining maturation (prāptaparipākaḥ), reaches supreme entitlement to the all-transcending sixfold scripture (sarvottīrṇabhagavatṣaḍardhaśāstraparamādhikāritām); another by leap-course (ullaṅghanakrameṇa) with endless difference (anantabhedena); some without sequence (akramam). (4) Hence: teachers of lower-lower doctrines (adharādharaśāsanasthā guravo 'pi) are non-entitled here (anadhikāriṇaḥ iha), even to mere maṇḍala-showing (maṇḍalamātradarśane 'pi); but a teacher of the upper doctrine (ūrdhvaśāsanasthas tu guruḥ), by fullness (pūrṇatvāt), enlivens even the lower-lower doctrine (adharādharaśāsanam prāṇayati) — hence all-entitled (sarvādhikārī). He is deśika, guru, ācārya, dīkṣaka, cumbaka — five names for one plenitude. And he, fully knowledgeable (pūrṇajñānaḥ eva), is supreme (sarvottamaḥ) — for without him (tena vinā) there is no success of initiation and the rest (dīkṣādyasampatteḥ).
terms: rājānugraha (royal favor), sarvādhikārin (all-entitled), daiśika/guru/ācārya/dīkṣaka/cumbaka (five teacher-names), srotaḥpañcaka (five streams), ṣaḍardhaśāstra (sixfold scripture).
function: Outsider mapping + teacher plenitude. Separates grace-presence from liberation-ending.
local_context: After grade-table (P4–P7); P8 maps outsiders; P9 takes up the yogin.
boundary: srotaḥpañcaka/ṣaḍardha technicals assumed (external). "Nature" renders svarūpa + prakṛti (AQ-3, L1 revision note).

body:
A yogin is fit to take on when he can deliver the goods at once, by teaching the means — fit in bare knowledge by that teaching, and in freedom too, by whoever comes close. Wanting fuller knowledge, take even many teachers, and move among them by the rank of their knowing. One thing forbidden: dropping a teacher who knows completely — that itself needs expiation. "But what of a teacher who goes silent, or teaches wrong?" Never: full knowledge means no lust or hate; the silence comes from something on the pupil's side (unfitness, distrust). Work harder at serving him; do not work at leaving him.

The passage moves in three steps. (1) The yogin's fitness: fit to take on (yuktaḥ) if, for one eager for fruit (phalotsukasya), able to give fruit immediately (avyavahitam eva phalaṃ dātum) through teaching of means (upāyopadeśena); through teaching of means, fit in knowledge alone (jñāne eva yuktaḥ), and in liberation too (mokṣe 'pi) through approaching (abhyupāyāt); desiring fullness of knowledge (jñānapūrṇatākāṅkṣī), may take even many teachers (bahūn api gurūn). (2) Conduct among teachers: according to differences of knowledge, higher and highest (uttamottamādijñānabhedāpekṣayā), one should conduct oneself (varteta) among them. But abandoning a teacher of complete knowledge (sampūrṇajñānagurutyāge) brings expiation itself (prāyaścittam eva). (3) The nanu + reply: "But is one who says nothing, or says the reverse, not to be abandoned?" (nanu so 'pi abruvan viparītaṃ vā bruvan kiṃ na tyājyaḥ?) — "Never" (naiva), we say (iti brūmaḥ). For by his very full knowledge (tasya hi pūrṇajñānatvāt eva) there is absence of passion and the rest (rāgādyabhāvaḥ). Hence silence and the rest must come from some cause residing in the pupil (śiṣyagatenaiva kenacit nimittena) — such as unfitness or distrust (ayogyatvānāśvastatvādinā). Hence the pupil must strive in his service (tadupāsane yatanīyam śiṣyeṇa), not in his abandonment (na tattyāge).
terms: phalotsuka (fruit-eager), avyavahita (without interval), upāyopadeśa (teaching of means), sampūrṇajñāna (complete knowledge), prāyaścitta (expiation), ayogyatva (unfitness), anāśvastatva (distrust).
function: Fitness rule, many-teacher rule, no-abandonment ruling (via nanu + reply).
boundary: None major (practical ruling). The reply's force depends on the premise (no rāga in the fully-knowing); if the premise fails, the ruling fails.

body:
The descent, cause of grace, is unconditioned — it does not wait on deeds or destinies. Concealment, by contrast, ripens thick suffering and confusion, all deed-conditioned. The mirror simile: the awake man playing the fool still inwardly despises folly; the fool playing awake, mouthing mantras, still despises the part — and the fool's acted awakeness, performed yet inwardly condemned, sinks him in the mud. For one in whom descent has risen, no hiding. And here too, stop weighing deeds — as before. Even then, will differs: one may yet taste suffering with this body (double-dealers, apostates). And even then, by that same differing will: the hidden one may join the descent himself — or, dead, through kin or teacher's grace. Holding to "the doings are mine, and I am the Lord" — never see the self as broken.

The passage moves in four steps. (1) Grace unconditioned: the descent (śaktipātaḥ), cause of grace (anugrahanimittam), is unconditioned indeed (nirapekṣaḥ eva) — disregarding karma, destiny, and the rest (karmādiniyatyapekṣaṇāt). (2) Concealment (tirobhāvaḥ): concealment has as its fruit (phalatva) the partaking in dense suffering and delusion (gāḍhaduḥkhamohabhāgitva) conditioned by karma and the rest (karmādyapekṣa). The mirror simile: by light's autonomy (prakāśasvātantryāt) the awakened (prabuddhaḥ) though behaving like the deluded (mūḍhavat ceṣṭate) inwardly censures deluded conduct (hṛdayena nindati mūḍhaceṣṭām); so the deluded (mūḍho 'pi) may perform awakened conduct such as mantra-worship (mantrārādhanādikām) and censure it (nindec ca). And as his deluded conduct, though performed (kriyamāṇāpi), perishes for the awakened (prabuddhasya dhvaṃsam eti) — so his awakened conduct, being censured (nindyamānā), of forbidden-conduct nature (niṣiddhācaraṇarūpatvāt), self-apprehensive through itself (svayaṃ ca tayā eva viśaṅkamānatvāt), drowns him (enam nimajjayati) in suffering-delusion-mud (duḥkhamohapaṅke). (3) But for one in whom descent has arisen (utpannaśaktipātasya tu) there is no concealment (na tirobhāvo 'sti). Here too, regard for karma is to be denied (niṣedhyā), as before (pūrvavat). There too, through will-diversity (icchāvaicitryāt): fruition of suffering with this body only (etaddehamātropabhogyaduḥkhaphalatvam vā) — as for those given to both service and censure toward initiation/conduct/teacher/god/fire (sevānindanobhayaprasaktānām iva) and as for former Śaiva-doctrine-dwellers who abandoned it (prāk śivaśāsanasthānāṃ tattyāginām iva). (4) There too, by will-diversity: though concealed (tirobhūto 'pi), one joins descent (yujyate) oneself (svayaṃ) by descent (śaktipātena), or dead (mṛto vā) through kin/teacher grace (bandhugurvādikṛpāmukhena). Thus (iti evaṃ) reflecting (anusaṃdadhat) act-partaking-in-oneself (kṛtyabhāgitvam svātmani) as the Lord itself (parameśvaraḥ eva), one should not see (na paśyet) the self as broken (khaṇḍitam ātmānam).
terms: anugraha (grace), tirobhāva (concealment), icchāvaicitrya (will-diversity), khaṇḍita (broken), kṛtyabhāgitva (act-partaking), bandhugurvādikṛpā (kin/teacher grace).
function: Closing of the ahnika: grace's final status, concealment, recovery, unbroken self.
boundary: "Mouthing mantras" (MT-009) is a register choice, flagged. "I am the Lord" (MT-010) self-reflexive made explicit [SUPPLIED-minor]. The mirror simile assumes everyday assent (mild, external).
